newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Compaq to use 300MHz Intel chip.
newsitem.headline: Compaq to use 300MHz Intel chip.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp said on Wednesday that it planned an autumn introduction of desktop computers powered by a 300 megahertz Pentium II processor from Intel Corp.

The chip is available now in workstations for engineers and scientists, and its arrival in desktop personal computers would maintain Intel's performance edge over rival chip makers Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Cyrix Corp.

Compaq planned to introduce the 300 megahertz desktops as part of an upgrade of its line of corporate PCs, said Bernd Orth, desktop division manager in Germany, at a strategy briefing in the Austrian Alps.
"We are very happy with the performance we get from Intel," he said when asked if Compaq's would use AMD chips. "Intel continues to move (processor) performance ahead."

Orth said Compaq this summer would introduce new Deskpro 2000 and 4000 desktops that use Pentium chips with MMX multimedia technology. New versions with Pentium II chips would follow in September or October, including a Deskpro 6000 running a 300 megahertz processor.
An Intel spokeswoman in Munich said the company had not yet announced plans to make the 300 megahertz Pentium II chip available for desktop PCs.

AMD and Cyrix this year began producing chips that for the first time reached the performance level of Intel's fastest chips. As their 200 megahertz chips were set to appear, Intel unexpectedly announced a 233 megahertz Pentium chip on June 2.
Increased competition has raised pricing pressure on all three companies.
On Tuesday AMD reported second quarter profit of seven cents per share -- well off the consensus estimate of 22 cents per share -- and cited the rapid shift toward new, high-performance processors.
Two weeks ago, Cyrix warned that it expected to post a loss in the second quarter as a result of weak demand and pricing pressures for its older products.
In May Intel warned that its second quarter results would not exceed the first quarter's levels, surprising investors. It blamed weak demand in Europe.
